earlier_scan.source_named: Extinct; only a wordlist (von den Steinen 1886) and comparative notes (Fargetti & Rodrigues 2008; Carvalho 2019); no phonological description exists.

sources.note: Lists only Fargetti & Rodrigues 2008 and Carvalho 2019 (both subclassification comments) and Ethnologue for the 'extinct' status; zero descriptive references.

sources.citation: Dixon, R. M. W. & Alexandra Y. Aikhenvald (eds.). 1999. The Amazonian Languages (Cambridge Language Surveys). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Chapters used: 4 Rodrigues 'Tupí', 5 Jensen 'Tupí-Guaraní', 6 Rodrigues 'Macro-Jê', 7 Barnes 'Tucano', 2 Derbyshire 'Carib', 13 Aikhenvald & Dixon 'Other small families and isolates'.
sources.note: Listed as the extinct third member of the Juruna branch; ch. 15 says the Manitsawá joined the Suyá and are now extinct. §2.3 'Tone' (p. 114) says 'there are two tones in the Monde branch, and in the Juruna language' -- about Juruna proper, not Manitsawá. Nothing on Manitsawá prosody.
Stub: 9 words attributed to Schuller 1911 (amatá, diadia, hayadi, madigaú..); nothing on phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey. 2024. Dicionário etimológico Tupi (parte I) — rascunho. Goiânia: Núcleo Takinahakỹ de Formação Superior Indígena, Universidade Federal de Goiás. Manuscript dated 4 Oct 2024, deposited by the author on the Internet Archive.
sources.note: Introduction says tones are marked for tonal languages and pre-modern forms are cited in chevrons with a source subscript; Manitsawá forms are reproduced with Steinen's acute marks but there is no remark anywhere on Manitsawá accent, stress or tone (all 8 Manitsawá citations screened; one footnote discusses Proto-Juruna tone from Yudjá/Xipaya reflexes, not Manitsawá).

sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey & Fernando O. de Carvalho. 2022. A revised reconstruction of the Proto-Tupian vowel system. Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi. Ciências Humanas 17(2): e20210035. doi:10.1590/2178-2547-BGOELDI-2021-0035.
sources.note: Nothing on Manitsawá prosody. Transcription conventions: 'The acute accent symbolizes the high tone in tonal languages (including the languages of the Mundurukú, Juruna, and Mondé branches, Karo, and maybe also Makurap); the low tone is left unmarked.. Data quoted from premodern sources, which are not expected to faithfully represent all the relevant phonological oppositions, are given verbatim enclosed in chevrons.. Forms in chevrons without subscript letters are from Steinen (1886) for Manitsawá'. The only Manitsawá datum discussed is ‹upá› 'Holz' (Steinen 1886: 361), cited for its vowel ('…

sources.citation: Jolkesky, Marcelo Pinho de Valhery. 2016. Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas. Tese de doutorado, Universidade de Brasília.
sources.note: Nothing: a text search of the whole 56 MB thesis finds 'Manitsawa' only in the classification tree (p. 800, p. ~813). No Manitsawá forms, no prosody. PDF downloaded to the work dir, searched, deleted; only the extract kept per the size/relevance rule.

sources.citation: Fargetti, Cristina Martins & Carmen L. Reis Rodrigues. 2008. Consoantes do Xipaya e do Juruna – uma comparação em busca do proto-sistema. Alfa (São Paulo) 52(2): 535-563.
sources.note: Nothing on Manitsawá stress. Manitsawá appears only as the extinct third member of the family: 'juntamente com o Manitsawá, já extinto (sobre o qual há apenas uma lista de palavras de STEINEN, 1942)' (p. 538) and 'Quanto ao povo manitsawá, nada se pode afirmar, não há relatos' (p. 540). The stress rule given on p. 545 ('Ocorre acento na primeira sílaba com tom alto da esquerda para a direita. Caso todos os tons sejam iguais, o acento recai sobre a última sílaba') is for Juruna/Yudja (yuru1259), not Manitsawá.

sources.citation: Rodrigues, Aryon Dall'Igna. 1986. Línguas brasileiras: para o conhecimento das línguas indígenas. São Paulo: Edições Loyola. 134 pp.
sources.note: Extinct Jurúna-family language ('do Manitsawá não temos mais que uma pequena lista de palavras'); no phonology, nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: Loukotka, Čestmír. 1968. Classification of South American Indian languages (ed. Johannes Wilbert). Los Angeles: Latin American Center, UCLA. 'Languages of the Yuruna group', p. 121 (entry 'Manitsauá or Mantizula' + comparative table column MANITSAUÁ).
sources.note: No phonology content; source list and a short comparative vocabulary with some accent marks carried over from Steinen (wordlist data only).

sources.citation: Simões, Mário F. 1963. Os "Txikão" e outras tribos marginais do alto Xingu. Revista do Museu Paulista, Nova Série 14: 76-104. São Paulo: Museu Paulista.
sources.note: Nothing. downloaded (9.6 MB, 34 pp., Acrobat Paper-Capture text) and read via extracted text. Ethnographic/ethnohistorical article on the Txikão and other 'marginal tribes' of the upper Xingu. Manitsawá appears only as an ethnonym: p. 77 lists 'Maritsava (Manitsawá)' among tribes of proven existence; footnote 1 (p. 77) says the Manitsawá, 'grupo tupi', lived on the rio Manitsauá (Manitsauá-missu), disappeared after Suyá and Jurúna attacks, Steinen met some as Suyá prisoners in 1884, informants told Vilas-Boas they fled up the Manitsauá to the Peixoto de Azevedo, 'Hoje são considerados extinto…

sources.citation: Rodrigues, Aryon Dall'Igna. 1955. As línguas "impuras" da família Tupí-Guaraní. In Herbert Baldus (ed.), Anais do XXXI Congresso Internacional de Americanistas (São Paulo, 1954), vol. II, pp. 1055-1071. São Paulo: Editora Anhembi. (Reprinted in Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica, periodicos.unb.br article 16256.)
sources.note: No phonology content for Manitsawá: §4.2 (p. 1060) only gives cognate percentages (Manitsawá-Yuruna 19/57 = 33%, Manitsawá-Šipaya 14/33 = 42%) and concludes it belongs to the Yuruna-Šipaya family, closer to Šipaya; calls the material 'extremamente reduzido'. No mention of acento/stress/tone for any Juruna-family language.

sources.citation: Nimuendajú, Curt. 1948. Tribes of the lower and middle Xingú River. In Julian H. Steward (ed.), Handbook of South American Indians, vol. 3: The Tropical Forest Tribes (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 143), pp. 213-243. Washington: Smithsonian Institution. Section 'Linguistic affinities', pp. 214-215.
sources.note: Classification and Yuruna~Shipaya sound correspondences (p ~ s, c ~ t, za ~ ya …) only; Manitsauá is mentioned solely as providing 'equivalents' that prove Tupí correspondences. Nothing on stress, accent or tone for any of the languages.

sources.citation: von den Steinen, Karl. 1942. O Brasil Central: expedição em 1884 para a exploração do Rio Xingu. Trad. Catarina Baratz Cannabrava. São Paulo: Companhia Editora Nacional (Brasiliana 3).
sources.note: Portuguese translation of the 1886 volume, the version cited as the Manitsawá wordlist by Fargetti & Rodrigues 2008; would only reproduce the same list and accent marks, so low value beyond the original already.

sources.citation: Loukotka, Čestmír. 1929. Le Šetá, un nouveau dialecte tupi. Journal de la Société des Américanistes 21(2): 373-398.
sources.note: Nothing about Manitsauá accent. Manitsauá figures as source siglum (p. 378: 'Man = Manitsauá : Steinen (Karl von den). — Du[r]ch Central Brasil[i]en. Leipzig, 1885, p. 360-361.'), as six cited forms inside the Šetá comparative vocabulary (pp. 381-387, e.g. 'Man iyabi-apá', 'Man huaya-dápa = pied', 'Man tanyayá = terre', with Steinen's final acute accents carried over), in the frequency table p. 395 (Manitsauá: 6 matches) and in the Tupi classification p. 398 ('IV. Tupi impurs : 1. Manitsáua, Yuruna, Kuruaya, Šipaya'). The only prosodic notation remark (p. 375 'à, é, í, ó, ú : voyelles accentu…

sources.citation: Schuller, Rodolpho R. 1911. Las lenguas indígenas de la Cuenca del Amazonas y del Orinoco. Revista Americana (Rio de Janeiro). Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú copy.
sources.note: No description of Manitsauá at all; only three Manitsauá words copied from von den Steinen inside long comparative lists (madigá 'luna', hayadí 'sol', itapa 'pescado'), reproducing Steinen's final-syllable accent marks. Wikipedia's 9-word 'Manitsauá vocabulary' is drawn from this.

sources.citation: von den Steinen, Karl. 1886. Durch Central-Brasilien: Expedition zur Erforschung des Schingú im Jahre 1884. Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus. Anhang V, section "VI. Manitsauá", pp. 360-361 (vocabulary), pp. 211-212 and 323-324 (how and from whom the words were elicited).
sources.note: The Manitsauá section gives only a vowel inventory (with nasalized ã ũ ĩ), a consonant table, one remark on medial clusters (tr, bl) and a 65-item wordlist; there is NO prose statement on Manitsauá accent. The wordlist itself carries an acute accent on nearly every item, almost always on the final syllable (humiá 'Haut', iyabiapá 'Haar', hayadí 'Sonne', madigaú 'Mond', hidagú 'Wasser', itapá 'Fisch', hayugú 'Hund', diadiá 'schwarz', anayú 'trinken'; exceptions: kele 'Steinbeil' unmarked, í-buá 'grün' double-marked). sources.citation: Carvalho, Fernando O. de. 2019. Revisitando o Proto-Jurúna: a reconstrução da série de oclusivas orais. In Oliveira, Vasconcelos & Sanches (eds.), Estudos Linguísticos na Amazônia, 215-236. Campinas: Pontes.

sources.note: Comparative-historical chapter; the only modern work Glottolog links to Manitsawá. May comment on the reliability and interpretation of von den Steinen's accent marks when using the list as comparative evidence. Unlikely to contain a stress rule.
